title: What AI Is Teaching Me About How Organizations Actually Work
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Patrick Dempsey opens a series on organizational dysfunction with a story about a university building whose ornamental shrubs grew until they blocked the light from every office, and nobody noticed because people simply brought in lamps. He uses it to describe his own institution's online course development process, which was designed more than a decade ago and has since accumulated steps, reviews, approvals, and handoffs until the process has become the work. His first thesis is that yesterday's solutions become today's problems, because every solution eventually creates a problem that needs another solution. He argues that many organizations function only because people have become skilled at working around the work. AI matters here not only as a way to trim the shrubs more efficiently but as a prompt to ask why the shrubs are being maintained at all. He previews a second thesis, that most of our work is work about work.
points: Organizations accumulate steps, approvals, and handoffs over time until keeping the process running becomes the job itself.
Every solution eventually becomes a problem that needs another solution, which produces what he calls loosely functioning disasters.
Workarounds for self-made work become the work, so people end up buying more lamps instead of cutting the shrubs down.
A process that works is not the same as a system that works well, and many institutions run on people's skill at working around it.
AI is most valuable as a reason to reconsider why the work exists, not only as a tool to make the existing work more efficient.
quotes: In a very real sense, the process has become the work. Everyone’s job is essentially making sure the process runs, which, of course, is in some sense essential!

Indeed, much of modern work consists of executing workarounds for the work we’ve created for ourselves. Eventually, those workarounds become the work, more workarounds are created, and without even knowing it, we’re working in the dark and buying more lamps instead of just cutting the freaking shrubs down!
I’ve often put it this way: Every solution to a problem eventually becomes a problem in need of another solution.
In fact, I’ve become increasingly convinced that many organizations function as “well” as they do because people have become extraordinarily skilled at working around the work!
AI isn’t just giving us better ways to trim the shrubs. It’s making us question why we’re maintaining them at all.
Of course, we’re going to use AI to make the work we do more efficient, but even more so we can use it to reconsider why the work exists in the first place.
But something working doesn’t necessarily mean the system supporting it works particularly well.
